chapter: Piano influences: Teddy Wilson, Tatum and Bud Powell
title: Billy Kyle and the John Kirby band
summary: He praises Kirby's tight classics-based band and Billy Kyle's underrated piano, which he links to Bud Powell's technique.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Do you want to get to Billy Kyle before you get into that?

Well, Billy Kyle was... I never met Billy Kyle, but I used to listen to him. Billy Kyle was with the band that was led by Maxine Sullivan's husband...John Kirby. John Kirby had a little band they called "the biggest little band in the land," I believe. It had Charlie Shavers on trumpet, Buster Bailey was the clarinetist, Russell Procope played the alto saxophone, John Kirby of course played bass, Billy Kyle was the pianist, and the drummer was an excellent drummer with the brushes, I think he'd been formerly with Cab Calloway and I can't think of his name...

Yes, it was. O'Neil Spencer, a very popular drummer then. But that was the tightest little band that I ever heard, and they made a specialty of playing some of the classics, things like some of Chopin's pieces, Edward Grieg, and these things that were arranged... I understand Charlie Shavers did most of the arranging. And they were really arranged in a very unique way. They also had a thing they used to play called "From A-Flat to C," which turned out to be a set of changes that a lot of musicians use now, which starts out on the augmented Fifth of the key that you're playing, and you go in progressions of fourths down to the original key. That was the first time I had ever heard that kind of a thing, was from that particular band, and the tune was called "From A Flat To C."

Billy Kyle had a style that I always felt like was like somewhere between Teddy Wilson and Earl Hines. He had the fast fingers like Teddy Wilson had, but he also had the punch of Earl Hines. With these different pianists, I would hear one, and for the next month or six weeks, I would be trying to play like him, and then next time you'd hear me, I'd be playing like somebody else. As a matter of fact, one time I even got on a thing where I used to use the pedal a lot and try to play like Lionel Hampton -- not like he plays the

piano, but to try to make the piano sound like a vibraharp! Which didn't turn out to be very successful. But a young guy learning like that, you begin to be... You are inspired by so many different people, you know. I guess in trying to grab a little of all of these people, you eventually come into your own with something.

But Billy Kyle was a very underrated pianist, an excellent pianist. But I don't think he ever really got some of the recognition that he should have gotten. A lot of times these things are due maybe to a person's personality -- I don't mean in an adverse way; I mean that maybe they just aren't as flamboyant as some other people. Or it could be that in fact you're working on a certain kind of job that doesn't display you as much as another job would. Nevertheless, Billy Kyle was a guy always worth listening to, and I...

I strongly feel that Bud Powell's style of playing was strongly influenced by Billy Kyle, as well as Charlie Parker. Because the way Bud Powell said things on the piano was like Charlie Parker, but his pianistic techniques a lot of times were a lot like Billy Kyle -- or a younger Billy Kyle, you'd

say. It always had a lot of punch and drive to it. So I guess that just about sums up that era, as far as I can think right now. But I might be jumping back in any time to say something about some incident that will probably come to mind.
